abstract: Conservation assessments of chronic anthropogenic disturbance increasingly ask whether changes in species composition translate into comparable changes in ecological function. This distinction is central to anticipating the long-term consequences of disturbance for ecosystem processes. Crude oil spills are a recurrent but understudied source of chronic disturbance in tropical freshwater ecosystems. We evaluated whether chronic oil contamination is associated with changes in taxonomic and functional diversity of anuran communities in six streams of the Narino coastal piedmont (Colombian Choco), within the area of influence of the Trans-Andean Pipeline. Amphibians are the most threatened vertebrate group worldwide and are particularly sensitive to both aquatic and terrestrial habitat degradation, making them sensitive indicators of chronic disturbance. We compared three oil-contaminated and three reference streams using standardized nocturnal surveys, Hill-number diversity, beta diversity, and multidimensional functional traits. We recorded 169 individuals from 24 species. Reference streams collectively contained more species and individuals than oil-contaminated streams, although coverage-standardized diversity varied substantially among individual streams and confidence intervals broadly overlapped. In contrast, functional diversity metrics, including functional richness, evenness, divergence, and trait composition, showed broad overlap between stream types. Overall, taxonomic patterns tended to favor reference streams, but these differences were not accompanied by a clear functional simplification, revealing a partial decoupling between taxonomic and functional responses consistent with high functional redundancy in one of the world's most biodiverse and chronically oil-exposed tropical regions. This decoupling underscores the need to incorporate functional, not only taxonomic, metrics into biodiversity impact assessments of chronic contamination in biodiversity hotspots.
